meta.title: Who really said "You Shall Either Die Upon the Gallows or of the Pox"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Disraeli. The earliest telling, in The European Magazine of January 1784, gives the line to Lord Sandwich and the retort to the actor Samuel Foote.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You Shall Either Die Upon the Gallows or of the Pox'?
meta.ogDescription: The gallows-or-the-pox insult is Lord Sandwich's, aimed at Samuel Foote in 1784. Gladstone and Disraeli were written into the anecdote by 1950.

answer.label: Not Benjamin Disraeli — Lord Sandwich, to Samuel Foote
answer.authorDates: 1718–1792 · First Lord of the Admiralty · named as the speaker in the earliest printed telling (January 1784)
answer.sourceLine: The line is the set-up half of a Georgian anecdote first printed in The European Magazine and London Review for January 1784, where Lord Sandwich needles the actor Samuel Foote and Foote fires back the famous reply about embracing his lordship’s mistress or his principles. Disraeli is not in that story at all — Quote Investigator ↗ finds the Gladstone-and-Disraeli casting no earlier than a 1950 American memoir, and even there Disraeli speaks the reply, not this line.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The European Magazine and London Review, vol. 5, January 1784

John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich — to the actor Samuel Foote (1720–1777)
Not documented before 1950, in George E. Allen’s Presidents Who Have Known Me

source.excerpt: Bon Mot of the late Sam. Foote — Sam. was invited to a convivial meeting at the house of the late Sir Francis Blake Delaval. Lord Sandwich was one of the guests upon the same occasion. When the Comedian entered, the Peer exclaimed, “what are you alive still?” “Yes, my Lord,” replied Foote. “Pray Sam,” retorted his Lordship, “which do you think will happen to you first, the experience of a certain disease, or an intimate acquaintance with the gallows?” “Why,” rejoined the Comedian, “that depends upon circumstances, and they are these, whether I prefer embracing your Lordship’s mistress, or, your principles.”
trail: January 1784 — the exchange appears as a memorial ‘bon mot’ of the recently dead Samuel Foote in The European Magazine and London Review ↗, with Lord Sandwich delivering the insult.

1809 — Percival Stockdale’s memoirs give the wording everyone now quotes, “you must either die of the p-x, or the halter,” still Sandwich to Foote; Wikiquote carries it ↗ from The Yale Book of Quotations.

1828–1844 — John Wilkes replaces Foote, first in a book on London’s clubs and then in Henry Brougham’s sketches, where Brougham cites the Duke of Norfolk as a witness but doubts the wording; Wikipedia calls the Wilkes attribution mistaken ↗.
1950 — Gladstone and Disraeli are written into the roles in George E. Allen’s memoir, the earliest such instance Quote Investigator could find ↗.
source.excerptNote: The blunter wording people quote today — the pox and the halter — comes from Percival Stockdale’s 1809 memoirs, which keep Sandwich and Foote but move the scene to the beefsteak club in Covent Garden. Wikiquote reproduces that version ↗, citing Stockdale via The Yale Book of Quotations.

source.rightsNote: Every documented telling of this line is old: the January 1784 European Magazine item, Percival Stockdale’s 1809 retelling, and the Victorian versions between them were all published long before 1931 and are in the public domain in the United States. The smoothed modern phrasing has no identified author. George E. Allen’s 1950 memoir, which first casts Gladstone and Disraeli, is still in copyright — but its wording is different and is not what is quoted here.

author.name: John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich
author.kicker: The man who threw the insult
author.heading: Who actually said it
author.metaLine: 1718–1792 · First Lord of the Admiralty · Georgian political grandee
author.bio: John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich, ran the Royal Navy through three spells as First Lord of the Admiralty, the last of them (1771–1782) covering the American War of Independence, and he is the peer the modern sandwich is named after ↗. He was also a reliable target for jokes about his morals: for years his mistress was Fanny Murray, the subject of John Wilkes’s scandalous Essay on Woman, which is exactly why the retort about ‘your lordship’s mistress’ landed. In this anecdote he is the aggressor, not the wit — the laugh belongs to Samuel Foote.

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-travelled anecdotes in English, and almost every retelling promotes the cast. Quote Investigator counts five proposed pairings; only the first is supported by an eighteenth-century printing.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ finds no Gladstone-and-Disraeli version earlier than George E. Allen’s 1950 memoir Presidents Who Have Known Me ↗, where Gladstone says Disraeli will “probably die by the hangman’s noose or a vile disease.” Disraeli died in 1881 ↗. Note too that even in this version Disraeli delivers the reply — so crediting him with the gallows line is wrong twice over, and the widely copied Disraeli version ↗ hands the insult to an unnamed Member of Parliament.

A book on the clubs of London put Wilkes in Foote’s place in 1828, and Henry Brougham repeated it in 1844, saying the Duke of Norfolk told him he was present — while himself doubting the words had come down accurately ↗. Wikipedia’s biography of Sandwich states plainly that the retort is often mistakenly attributed to Wilkes ↗.

An undated theatrical joke collection, catalogued by HathiTrust at about 1816, gives the exchange to the actor James Quin and an unnamed nobleman. Quin died in 1766, and QI notes the ascription appeared many years after his death ↗, which badly weakens it.

items.who: The Earl of Sandwich and Charles James Fox
items.why: An MP alluded to the story in the House of Commons in 1968 with Fox as the target, giving only the first line — another late substitution recorded in QI’s chronology ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest known printing — The European Magazine, January 1784 ↗ — puts the gallows-and-disease line in Lord Sandwich’s mouth and the retort in Samuel Foote’s.

context.heading: Why this joke keeps changing hands
lead: Some jokes are too good to leave attached to a half-remembered actor. This one has been re-cast at least five times in two hundred and forty years: Sandwich and Foote in 1784, an unnamed nobleman and James Quin by about 1816, Sandwich and John Wilkes from 1828, Gladstone and Disraeli by 1950, and Sandwich and Charles James Fox when an MP alluded to it in the Commons in 1968. Each retelling swaps in bigger names, which is exactly how a famous line ends up on the wrong mouth.

The 1784 version is also the funniest, because it is the most specific. Foote had died in 1777 and the magazine ran the item as a memorial ‘bon mot of the late Sam. Foote’; the setting is a supper at Sir Francis Blake Delaval’s, and the jab about Sandwich’s mistress was pointed rather than generic. Strip out the names and the room, as later versions do, and you are left with a portable gag that will attach itself to whichever pair of rivals the reader already has in mind.
detailsBody: The 1784 text has Sandwich ask “which do you think will happen to you first, the experience of a certain disease, or an intimate acquaintance with the gallows?” The blunter phrasing everyone quotes — the pox and the halter — comes from Percival Stockdale’s 1809 memoirs, which relocate the scene to the beefsteak club in Covent Garden but keep Sandwich and Foote.

The modern internet form drifts further still. A widely copied version credited to Disraeli has an unnamed Member of Parliament deliver the insult and Disraeli answer “whether I embrace your policies or your mistress” — policies for principles, which quietly kills the pun the joke was built on.
context.pull: Disraeli did not say it, and in the version that names him he is not even the one saying this half.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator lists five proposed pairings, gives January 1784 The European Magazine (Sandwich to Samuel Foote) as the earliest evidence located, records the Wilkes version from 1828 and Brougham 1844, a James Quin version catalogued c. 1816, the Gladstone–Disraeli version in George E. Allen's 1950 book, and a 1968 Commons allusion naming Charles James Fox; it concludes Foote is the leading candidate for the riposte.

The Internet Archive holds The European Magazine and London Review, vol. 5, January 1784, and its scanned text contains the 'Bon Mot of the late Sam. Foote' item with Lord Sandwich asking which will happen first, 'the experience of a certain disease, or an intimate acquaintance with the gallows'.

Wikiquote's Samuel Foote page reproduces the exchange in the Percival Stockdale (1809) wording — 'you must either die of the p-x, or the halter' — citing Stockdale's Memoirs via The Yale Book of Quotations (2006).

Wikipedia's article on John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich (13 November 1718 – 30 April 1792; First Lord of the Admiralty 1748–51, 1763, 1771–82) reproduces the Sandwich–Foote exchange, states 'This retort is often mistakenly attributed to John Wilkes', says the modern sandwich is named after him, and notes Fanny Murray was his mistress.

Garson O'Toole's October 2012 post to the American Dialect Society list reports the 1784 European Magazine citation with Lord Sandwich and Samuel Foote as the earliest he had found, and invites earlier cites.
George E. Allen's Presidents Who Have Known Me was published by Simon and Schuster in 1950 and is held by the Internet Archive.

A widely copied online version credits Benjamin Disraeli, with an unnamed Member of Parliament saying 'Sir, you will either die on the gallows or of some unspeakable disease' and Disraeli replying 'whether I embrace your policies or your mistress'.
Benjamin Disraeli was born 21 December 1804 and died 19 April 1881.
Samuel Foote was a dramatist, actor and theatre manager, January 1720 – 21 October 1777.
